subject: Problem with sightings rounded to distance zero

messages.author: cf5944c821060323
messages.subject: Problem with sightings rounded to distance zero
parts:
I have a situation in which I suspect sightings rounded to distance zero are leading to a sub-optimal detection function. In your opinion, is the problem severe enough in this particular situation (see below) to require attention, and what is the appropriate way to address it?

 

I have ~600 sightings of North Atlantic right whales sighted from a Twin Otter aircraft on surveys of the southeast U.S coast. The plane few at 1000 ft; position and altitude were logged with GPS every few seconds. There were two observers with bubble windows, allowing visibility of the trackline. From what I can tell, the survey protocol was designed and executed with distance sampling in mind. However, observers did not collect perpendicular distance measurements (e.g. with inclinometers). Instead, the aircraft broke from the trackline, overflew the sighted group and marked it with GPS.

 

Using trigonometry, I calculated perpendicular distance to that “actual position” from the trackline vector estimated from 30 seconds of position points logged up to the break to circle the sighting. 633 sightings remained after right truncation. A hazard rate detection function fitted to these showed a spike at the shortest distance bin and the QQ plot showed slight bias at close distances (see attached cds_hr.pdf and .txt). (There were also notably short bins at about 600 and 1500 meters, but I suspect these are random.)

 

On investigation, I found that 33 sightings had a distance of exactly zero. For these sightings, it appeared the survey team pressed the “actual position” button in their software before breaking from the trackline. In several cases they logged messages similar to “Whale surfaced directly under the plane!”

 

My suspicion is that in these “directly under the plane” events, most of the sightings were not exactly on the trackline but the team did not see a need to overfly the sighting again to collect a post-break “actual position”. As a consequence, the distances of these were all exactly zero, because the actual positions were logged while still exactly on the trackline.

 

As an experiment, I left truncated the data at a distance of 1 m and fitted the detection function again. 34 sightings were removed: the 33 at distance 0 and one more at distance 0.032 which is based on a post-break overflight. This removed the spike from the closest distance bin and the deviation from the diagonal on the QQ plot (see attached cds_hr_with_left_trunc.pdf and .txt). Goodness of fit statistics generally improved. But estimated abundance went down from 1332 (CV=0.052) to 1176 (CV=0.051).

 

What do you believe is the best thing to do in this case? Left truncation certainly improves the fit of the detection function but arguably results in an underestimation of abundance. The 33 sightings at distance zero should have been spread over a larger distance and then counted in the estimate. Instead they were discarded. The width of the survey remained essentially the same (smaller by 1 meter), so estimated density will be significantly less.

 

I suppose if I could plausibly estimate the range of distances those sightings were likely to be spread over, I could left truncate at that outermost distance, or try to smear the sightings somehow. But that seems complicated and I’m not really certain how to estimate that distance range.

 

Thanks for your thoughts,

 

Jason

messages.author: 9b03386432b784c0
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Problem with sightings rounded to distance zero
parts:
Hi Jason, list,

The way I see it, Distance was able do do the right thing without the left truncation, i.e. it cut through the spike. That is not surprising, since the small number of parameters that the model includes would not be able to fit it any way. So the density estimate is probably reasonable, even if the GOF statistics say it's a bad fit. It is a bad fit, but you know why. I agree the other dips and spikes might just be spurious, even though with 633 sightings I would not really expect such strong patterns in some specific bands, as you say around 600 and 1500m, but the way you described the distances are obtained, can't think of another obvious explanation (unless there was some partially blind spot?). So possibly you really only have a problem in terms of GOF, but no real bias, so you could just simply ignore it.

Or, if you prefer not to do that, and get nicer looking detection function plots and GOF stats, you could also just bin the data. I suspect that if you bin the data into 250 m bins, which just assumes that all those 0's would be within 250 m from the line, which seems reasonable given your description of the physics involved, (I suspect) you will get a little loss of precision, if any, and a very similar estimate to that obtained with all the data...

Hope this helps, maybe others have additional thoughts (if you implement any of this let me know what happens  - possibly on the side if not relevant to the list)

Tiago
